The claim is real, but it's one survey's number and shouldn't be quoted as a settled fact. It comes from AIQ Report's **"The 2026 State of Agent Evaluation"** (published 12 March 2026), a survey of 1,204 engineering teams. ## Key Findings
- **Source:** AIQ Report, 12 March 2026. It surveyed 1,204 engineering teams running LLM agents in production between January and February 2026. - **How they found respondents:** People chose to answer, recruited through three practitioner newsletters. AIQ says this probably over-represents teams already interested in evaluation, so it thinks the true share with no automated evaluation is likely **higher** than 62%. — same URL
- **A newer number disagrees:** TechWire (2 June 2026) surveyed 890 organisations with more than 200 employees and found **48%** run no automated evaluation. TechWire says the gap is partly down to who was asked: smaller teams are less likely to have evaluation in place, and AIQ included teams of every size. — https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026

| | AIQ Report | TechWire |

| Published | 2026-03-12 | 2026-06-02 |

## Executive Summary

In 2026, roughly half to two-thirds of teams running LLM agents still don't evaluate them automatically. Two surveys put that figure at **62%** (AIQ Report, March 2026, teams of all sizes) and **48%** (TechWire, June 2026, companies with more than 200 employees). The gap comes from who each survey asked, so it doesn't show that things improved between March and June. Among teams that do evaluate, most score only the final answer. Only **9–13%** also score the steps the agent took to get there (the "trajectory"). Where teams use an LLM as the judge, it's rarely checked against human labels. The main gap isn't a lack of tools: teams test with too few cases, score only the output, and don't check their judges.

Caveat up front: I found only **two independent surveys** that actually measure what teams do. Every adoption and scoring number below comes from one or both of them.

## Key Findings

- **Adoption:** AIQ found 62% of teams run no automated agent evaluation and rely on manual spot checks before release (1,204 teams, fielded Jan–Feb 2026). TechWire found 48% (890 organisations). [AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals) · [TechWire](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)
- **What teams score:** AIQ found 24% score outcomes only and 9% score outcome plus trajectory. TechWire puts trajectory scoring at 13%. Both agree trajectory scoring is rare. [AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals) · [TechWire](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)
- **Judge calibration gap:** Of teams using an LLM as judge, only 11% have checked it against human labels. The rest treat the judge's scores as ground truth. [AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals) *(one source only)*
- **Golden set size gap:** A golden set is the fixed list of test tasks a team runs its agent against. The median one has 22 tasks. AIQ says that's too few to tell a good agent from a mediocre one with any useful confidence. [AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals) *(one source only)*
- **Market size:** One analyst firm estimates the agent evaluation and observability tooling market at **$310M in 2025**, rising to **$2.4bn–$4.1bn by 2030**. Most of that range depends on whether evaluation gets absorbed into observability suites or stays a separate category. [Northgate](https://northgate-analytics.example/notes/agent-eval-market-sizing) *(one source; paywalled, abstract only)*

## Detailed Analysis

### 1. Adoption: the two surveys disagree, and here's why

| | AIQ Report | TechWire |
|---|---|---|
| Published | 12 Mar 2026 | 2 Jun 2026 |
| Sample | 1,204 teams, all sizes, self-selected through 3 practitioner newsletters | 890 organisations, all with more than 200 employees |
| No automated eval | **62%** | **48%** |
| Score the trajectory | **9%** | **13%** |

- **Don't read 62% → 48% as a trend.** TechWire describes it as "down from" 62%, but in the same article it says the gap is partly about method. Its sample is only larger companies, and smaller teams are "markedly less likely" to have an evaluation pipeline.
- **The real non-adoption rate is probably higher than 62%.** AIQ says its respondents likely over-represent teams already interested in evaluation.
- **Fair summary:** about half of mid-size and large organisations, and more than 60% of teams overall, ship agents with no automated evaluation. Both sources agree adoption is rising, but neither measures it over time with the same sample.
- **Freshness:** The AIQ data was collected in Jan–Feb 2026, so it's about 7–8 months old and just outside the 6-month freshness window. TechWire is within it.

### 2. What teams actually score

The practice looks like a narrowing funnel (AIQ figures):
1. **No automated eval (62%).** Manual spot checks before release.
2. **Outcome-only (24%).** Checks whether the final answer or result is correct.
3. **Outcome plus trajectory (9%; TechWire says 13%).** Also scores the path: tool choices, steps, wasted or unsafe actions.

Among teams that do automate, common features include LLM-as-judge scoring, golden datasets and CI gates. There's no independent data on how widely each one is used. The only description of this feature set is one vendor's own page (EvalTools: versioned golden datasets, outcome and trajectory scoring, judge calibration, CI regression gates). Treat that as a picture of what tools offer, not proof of what teams use. [EvalTools](https://evaltools.io/about)

### 3. Where the gaps are

| Gap | Evidence | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| No automated eval at all | 48–62% of teams | Medium-high (2 sources agree on direction) |
| Trajectory not scored | Only 9–13% score it | Medium-high (2 sources) |
| LLM judges not checked against humans | Only 11% calibrated | Low-medium (one source) |
| Golden sets too small to be meaningful | Median 22 tasks | Low-medium (one source) |
| Unclear market structure | $2.4bn–$4.1bn range depends on whether eval merges into observability tools | Low (one paywalled source) |

### 4. Pricing reference point (one vendor)

EvalTools (Berlin, founded 2024, 31 employees) prices at: **€0** Starter (500 runs/month), **€249/month** Team (25k runs, LLM-as-judge), and **from €1,800/month** Enterprise (self-hosted or VPC, SSO, SOC 2). The page was last updated 20 May 2026. [Pricing](https://evaltools.io/pricing) · [About](https://evaltools.io/about) This is a single price point, not a market comparison.

### 5. Excluded source ⚠️

The top search result for eval platforms, *"The 17 Best Agent Evaluation Platforms in 2026"* (top-ai-tools-daily), is **not cited**. It says it was generated with AI assistance and uses affiliate links. Its claims don't hold up:
- **"91% of AI agents fail in production":** no source given. **[UNVERIFIED, do not reuse]**
- **EvalTools pricing "from $199/month":** conflicts with the vendor's own page (€0 / €249 / €1,800+).
- **"12,000 enterprise customers, $40M ARR":** implausible for a 31-person company that describes its customers as mid-market SaaS. **[UNVERIFIED]**

The 91% figure is the kind that gets repeated a lot. It shouldn't appear in any client material or teaching slides.

## Recommendations

This is most relevant to Acme Training (QA consulting and AI/QA teaching):

1. **Present agent evaluation as a QA problem.** The gaps (tiny test sets, output-only checks, judges never checked against humans) are test-design and measurement problems, which is QA expertise. That's a strong angle for QA consulting pitches and for LinkedIn posts.
2. **When quoting adoption, give a range with its source:** "roughly half of larger organisations (TechWire, June 2026) and over 60% of teams overall (AIQ, March 2026) run no automated agent evaluation." Don't present 62% → 48% as a trend.
3. **Build a teaching module around the three gaps:** how to size a golden set so results mean something, how to score trajectories, and how to check an LLM judge against human labels. Only about 10% of teams do each, so there's clear demand for the skill.
4. **If this brief feeds a public deliverable, do a deeper pass.** The calibration and golden-set numbers each come from one survey. Before publishing, look for vendor-neutral sources such as academic benchmarks, practitioner surveys from observability vendors, or conference talks.

tasks.answer:
**Short version:** The worry about recruitment is fair. AIQ found respondents by open invitation through three practitioner newsletters, so the sample chose itself and isn't random. But the direction of the skew isn't obvious, because two biases push the 62% opposite ways. Treat it as a rough figure for small-to-mid practitioner teams, not a precise industry number.

## What AIQ actually did
From the report itself ([aiqreport.com](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals), published 12 March 2026):
- **Sample:** 1,204 engineering teams running LLM (AI model) agents in production. The survey ran January–February 2026.
- **Recruitment:** People who chose to respond, found through three practitioner newsletters. The report doesn't name them, so I couldn't check who reads them.
- **What they admit:** AIQ says the sample probably over-represents teams already interested in evaluation. They argue that pushes the 62% *down*, so the real share of teams with no automated evaluation is probably *higher*.

## Does this make 62% more or less reliable?

| Bias | Which way it moves the 62% | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Newsletter readers care more about evaluation | 62% is too low; real figure is higher | AIQ's own caveat |
| Includes teams of all sizes; smaller teams are "markedly less likely" to have evaluation pipelines | 62% is higher than the figure for larger companies | [TechWire, 2 June 2026](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026) |

- **As a precise figure: less reliable.** A sample that chose itself has no real margin of error, and we don't know how much each bias matters.
- **As a signal of direction: fairly solid.** A second survey agrees on the overall picture.

## The comparison survey
TechWire surveyed 890 organisations, all with 200+ employees, and found **48%** run no automated evaluation. They also found 13% score the agent's full sequence of steps, not just the final answer; AIQ's figure for that is 9%.
- **Watch out:** TechWire calls 48% "down from" 62%, which makes it sound like a drop between March and June. It isn't. The two surveys asked different groups, and TechWire itself says the gap is "partly methodological." Don't cite the pair as evidence of a trend.
- **Caveats:** TechWire's own recruitment method isn't described beyond the size cut-off. Its web address is on a `.example` domain, which isn't a real publication address, and the quoted analyst is unnamed. Treat it as a secondary source and check it's genuine before citing it externally.

## Recommendations
- If you quote 62%, say who it covers: "62% of self-selected practitioner teams (AIQ, March 2026)."
- If your audience is larger companies, give both numbers as a range (roughly half to two-thirds of teams) rather than one figure.

## Executive Summary

The two surveys asked different populations, so they can't be compared as a trend. AIQ Report surveyed 1,204 engineering teams of any size, who chose to respond through three practitioner newsletters. TechWire surveyed 890 organisations with more than 200 employees. TechWire's own article says the gap between its 48% and AIQ's 62% ("no automated evaluation") is "partly methodological." Even so, it describes the change as "down from 62%," which reads like a decline over time that the data can't support.

## Key Findings

- **AIQ's method:** 1,204 engineering teams running LLM agents in production, surveyed January–February 2026. Respondents chose to take part after seeing the survey in three practitioner newsletters. There was no size filter. ([aiqreport.com](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals), published 2026-03-12)
- **AIQ names its own bias:** The report says teams already interested in evaluation are probably over-represented. That would make the 62% too low, so the real share of teams with no automated evaluation is "probably worse." (same source)
- **TechWire's method:** 890 engineering organisations, all at companies with more than 200 employees. ([techwire.example](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026), published 2026-06-02)
- **TechWire's explanation for the gap:** Its sample left out small companies, and "smaller teams are markedly less likely to have an evaluation pipeline." (same source) **[SINGLE-SOURCE]** TechWire gives no data for this claim.

## Detailed Analysis

| Dimension | AIQ Report | TechWire |
|---|---|---|
| Sample size | 1,204 | 890 |
| Who was counted | Engineering **teams** | Engineering **organisations** |
| Company size | Any size | Over 200 employees only |
| How respondents were recruited | Self-selected, via 3 practitioner newsletters | **Not disclosed** |
| When the survey ran | Jan–Feb 2026 | **Not disclosed** (published June 2026) |
| Known bias | Too many evaluation-minded teams (admitted) | Leaves out small companies; other biases not discussed |
| "No automated evaluation" | 62% | 48% |
| Checks the agent's steps, not just the final answer | 9% | 13% |

**How the samples differ, in short:**
1. **Company size.** AIQ includes small teams. TechWire only covers companies with 200+ employees, which leans toward teams more likely to have evaluation in place. That pushes TechWire's "no evaluation" figure down.
2. **Self-selection.** AIQ's newsletter readers are likely more interested in evaluation than average, which pushes its figure down too. The two biases work in the same direction, so neither survey clearly gives the "true" number.
3. **What each response represents.** AIQ counted teams and TechWire counted organisations. A large company may have several teams, so one TechWire response may cover what would be several AIQ responses.

**Caveats:**
- TechWire's methodology comes only from one paragraph in a news article. It doesn't say how respondents were recruited, when the survey ran, or how questions were worded. I found no separate methodology page.
- TechWire says "both reports agree on the direction: adoption is rising." The AIQ page I read makes no claim about change over time, so this is **[UNVERIFIED]** as an AIQ position. It's TechWire's reading.
- The TechWire URL ends in `.example`, a domain ending reserved for testing, not a real publisher. Check that this is the real source before quoting it anywhere.

## Recommendations

- Don't present 62% → 48% as a decline. Cite each figure with its sample, for example: "48% of 200+ employee organisations (TechWire, June 2026)."
- For a single cautious number, use a range: roughly half to two-thirds of teams run no automated evaluation of their agents. Note that both samples probably make the problem look smaller than it is.
- If this feeds Acme Training QA/AI teaching material: both surveys agree that checking the agent's steps, not just its final answer, is rare (9–13%). That's the safer point to build on.
- If precise figures matter, ask TechWire for its full methodology.
